image_description: An underwater close-up shot of a large cetacean, specifically focusing on the head and anterior body. The skin is dark grey/black with significant mottling and white patches indicative of barnacles or cyamids. A broad pectoral flipper is visible near the bottom left. The lighting is dim, typical of deep water, with some particulate matter suspended in the blue-green water.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Head is relatively short with arched rostrum and two blowholes on top.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image is a side-profile close-up of the lower head and jaw area; the top of the rostrum and blowholes are outside the frame or obscured by the angle.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Skin is mottled grey to greyish-black with distinctive white patches from barnacles and whale lice.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible skin clearly exhibits the characteristic mottled pattern with numerous white spots/patches consistent with barnacle encrustation found on grey whales.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: No dorsal fin present; multiple dorsal knuckles along posterior back.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The dorsal region (back) is not visible in this head-focused shot; only the side of the head and shoulder area are shown.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Robust spindle-shaped body of enormous proportions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: While the full body isn't visible, the curvature of the head and shoulder suggests a massive, robust structure consistent with a large baleen whale.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Skin is mottled grey with white patches created by barnacles.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed again on the visible upper body/head section; texture matches the diagnostic criteria perfectly.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Baleen plates are cream-colored, densely packed in numerous rows along each side.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The mouth is closed or the angle does not reveal the interior oral cavity where baleen plates would be located.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Flippers (pectoral fins) are broad and paddle-shaped, remarkably elongated relative to body size.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: A large, broad flipper is clearly visible in the lower-left quadrant. Its shape and attachment point are anatomically correct for a grey whale.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail flukes are broad with smooth trailing edge and central notch.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The tail is completely outside the frame.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Skin texture is rough with callosities.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The high-resolution crop shows a rough, uneven surface texture with raised bumps (callosities/barnacles), matching the biological description.

alignment_reasoning: The image strongly aligns with the 'grey whale' class. All testable checkpoints regarding skin texture, mottling patterns, and flipper morphology are present and accurate. Several key diagnostic features (blowholes, dorsal knuckles, baleen, tail) are untestable due to the tight framing/cropping, but there are no contradictions in the visible data. The visual evidence is highly specific to Eschrichtius gibbosus.
artifact_reasoning: No AI-generation artifacts detected. The image exhibits natural underwater lighting falloff, realistic particulate scattering, and coherent biological textures. Edges are sharp where in focus, and there is no structural melting or anatomical impossibility.
